title: Les Paul & Leo Fender Part I
summary: Part one of a two-part episode on the invention of the electric guitar, focused on the rivalry and parallel work of Leo Fender and Les Paul. The hosts cover the difficulty of naming a single inventor, George Beauchamp and the 1931 Rickenbacker "frying pan" lap steel, the feedback problem of hollow acoustic "Spanish" guitars, and Fender's background as a radio repairman and engineer who never trained formally. The Les Paul section covers his childhood tinkering (including amplifying his guitar with a phonograph needle), his Gibson connections and the rejected "Log" prototype, his Los Angeles career with Bing Crosby, his electrocution injury, World War Two service, sound-on-sound multitrack recording, and his first meeting with Fender through a steel guitarist. The episode ends with a cliffhanger promising a gentleman not yet introduced in part two.
topics: Stuff You Should Know part one

segments.title: Opening and framing the electric guitar story
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the two-part episode, credit the book The Birth of Loud by Ian Port, and discuss why the electric guitar's invention is hard to attribute to one person.
topics: Stuff You Should Know part one

segments.title: Leo Fender's early life and engineering background
segments.summary: Leo Fender is described as an engineer who lost an eye as a child, taught himself by tinkering, and built radios and public address systems, which grew into a repair shop in Fullerton, California.

segments.title: Early electric instruments and pickups
segments.summary: The hosts explain pickups and the electromagnetic principle behind them, the 1931 Rickenbacker lap steel 'frying pan' tied to George Beauchamp, and the distinction between early electric guitars and the first solid body electric guitar.

segments.title: Feedback problem and the goal of louder guitars
segments.summary: Hollow-body acoustic 'Spanish' guitars with pickups fed back at high volume, so guitars could not cut through horns, drums and vocals; Fender set out to solve this.

segments.title: Les Paul's childhood and early tinkering
segments.summary: Les Paul, born Lester Polsfuss in Waukesha, Wisconsin, is introduced as a performer and tinkerer. As a teen he reportedly amplified his guitar using a phonograph needle and radio, and he played in a country and harmonica act.

segments.title: Gibson, the Log, and the rejected solid body prototype
segments.summary: Les Paul's Gibson connections and electrified Spanish models such as the ES-150 are discussed. He built the Log, a pine block with a neck and a homemade pickup, and Gibson in Kalamazoo reportedly rejected it. The Log is displayed at the Waukesha County Museum.

segments.title: Fender's Esquire-style prototype and early Fender work
segments.summary: Leo Fender's early solid body prototype, which he built to test pickups and the solid body concept, is described. Bands rented it for shows, and Fender went on to build amps and grow his company.

segments.title: Les Paul's career, injury, war service and multitrack recording
segments.summary: Les Paul's Los Angeles career with Bing Crosby, a 1948-era electrocution injury, Army service during World War Two, the hit It's Been a Long Long Time, and his sound-on-sound multitrack recording technique using acetate discs. Leo Fender and Les Paul are introduced through a steel guitarist, and the hosts tease part two.
topics: World War Two Armed Forces Radio

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close part one and promote part two on Thursday.
